entities.name: Corc mac Luigthig
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Corc mac Luigthig (c. 340–379 CE) stands as a pivotal, albeit semi-legendary, figure in the early history of Ireland, recognized as the progenitor of the powerful Eóganachta dynasty, which would dominate the kingship of Munster for over six centuries. Operating during the late Classical era, a period marked by the decline of Roman power in Britain and the rise of distinct Gaelic kingdoms, Corc is credited with consolidating power in the southern half of Ireland, laying the foundational structures for a regional hegemony that profoundly shaped medieval Irish political and social landscapes. His reign marks a crucial transition from a fragmented tribal system to a more centralized, dynastic form of kingship, establishing precedents for royal succession and territorial control.

The core events attributed to Corc involve the establishment of Cashel (Caiseal Mumhan) as the royal seat of Munster, a strategic move that provided a focal point for the nascent kingdom and a powerful symbol of Eóganachta authority. While specific historical details of his life are intertwined with later genealogical and mythological narratives, tradition recounts his travels abroad, including a period in Scotland, which may reflect early interactions between Gaelic peoples across the Irish Sea. Upon his return, Corc is said to have asserted his dominance over rival tribes, uniting various disparate groups under his banner and initiating the dynastic lineage that would produce numerous kings of Munster and, eventually, High Kings of Ireland.
